title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Expand, Migrate, Contract
intro: Code can be rolled back in seconds; a database schema change can't. And during a rolling deploy, old and new code run side by side against the same database. The task: rename the column users.fullname to display_name without downtime. Doing it in one step ('ALTER TABLE ... RENAME') breaks every old pod the moment it runs. The safe way takes several deploys.

steps.prompt: Expand: add the new column display_name (text, nullable) to users. Protect the site by giving up if the table lock can't be had within 3 seconds.
expected_commands: psql -c "SET lock_timeout = '3s'; ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;"
psql -c "SET lock_timeout='3s'; ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;"
steps.explanation: A new, empty, nullable column. Old code doesn't know about it and isn't affected.
steps.why: Adding a nullable column is quick and backwards-compatible. The lock_timeout matters: ALTER TABLE needs a brief exclusive lock, and if a long-running query holds the table, the ALTER waits, and every other query queues up behind it. Without a timeout, a 'harmless' migration takes the site down. With one, it fails fast and you retry.

steps.prompt: Deploy code that writes to BOTH columns. Then backfill existing rows in small batches rather than one giant UPDATE: run the first batch of 10,000.
expected_commands: psql -c "UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE display_name IS NULL LIMIT 10000);"
steps.explanation: 10,000 rows copied; repeat until none are left.
steps.why: One UPDATE over 50 million rows holds locks for minutes, bloats the table, and floods the replicas with changes (replication lag). Small batches with a pause between them keep the database healthy. The dual-write deploy has to come first, or rows changed during the backfill would be missed.

steps.prompt: Verify the backfill is complete before going further: count rows where display_name is still NULL.
expected_commands: psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE display_name IS NULL;"
psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE display_name IS NULL"
steps.explanation: Every row has the new column filled.
steps.why: Each phase has a check before the next begins. Now you can deploy code that reads from display_name (still writing both), then code that stops writing fullname. Each of those deploys can be rolled back on its own, because the database still satisfies the previous version.

steps.prompt: Contract: only after no deployed code reads or writes fullname, and a few days have passed, drop the old column.
expected_commands: psql -c "SET lock_timeout = '3s'; ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN fullname;"
psql -c "SET lock_timeout='3s'; ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN fullname;"
steps.why: This is the one step you can't undo, which is why it comes last and after a waiting period. If you'd dropped it in the same release that stopped using it, a rollback of that release would hit a missing column.

steps.prompt: In the pipeline, migrations run as a separate step before the new code rolls out. Check which migrations have been applied (the project uses Alembic).
steps.explanation: The schema is at the latest migration.
steps.why: Migration tools (Alembic, Flyway, Liquibase, Rails migrations) record which changes have run, so every environment reaches the same schema in the same order. Run them as a distinct pipeline step, not on application start-up: ten pods starting at once shouldn't race to migrate. The whole pattern has one rule: every schema change must be compatible with both the previous and the next version of the code.
